label: Title
notes: Open by putting the section in one sentence: for convex functions, ordinary differentiability is the collapse of every supporting certificate to one vector. The title visual should already preview the whole lecture route. A smooth point has one support, a corner has many, and the directional derivatives tell the same story from a different angle.

label: Unique Supporting Hyperplane
notes: Use the epigraph picture before the formula. The ordinary derivative gives a linear first-order model, while convexity asks for affine lower supports. At a differentiable point those two roles merge: the gradient vector defines the only support that can touch at the point and remain below the function everywhere.

label: Singleton Subdifferential
notes: State the theorem as the section's hinge. The forward direction is quick once the directional derivative is linear, but the reverse direction is the convex-analysis insight: a unique subgradient rules out first-order directional spread. Also flag the domain consequence, because a finite differentiability point must actually sit in the interior of the effective domain.

label: Directional Collapse
notes: Make the directional derivative feel like a support function. In general it is sublinear because it is the support function of the subdifferential. When the subdifferential collapses to one point, the support function becomes a linear pairing. The coordinate partial derivative criterion is powerful precisely because convexity fills in the rest of the directions.

label: Smooth Bowl Example
notes: Use the quadratic bowl as the clean baseline. Every tangent plane is unique, the directional derivative is just the dot product with the displayed gradient, and finite differences behave exactly as students expect. This gives a reference point before the lecture moves to examples where convexity keeps supports valid but destroys uniqueness.

label: Absolute Value Corner
notes: This is the smallest warning example. The absolute value corner is convex, and every supporting slope in the interval is legitimate. A numerical central difference at the corner can return zero, but that does not certify differentiability. The real test is whether all directional slopes combine into one linear map, and they do not.

label: Max Ridge
notes: Move from the one-dimensional corner to a two-dimensional ridge. Away from the line where the affine pieces tie, one plane wins and the gradient is clear. Along the ridge, both planes are active, so the subdifferential is the convex hull of their gradients. The directional derivative is a maximum, which is sublinear but not linear.

label: Almost Everywhere Intuition
notes: Give the almost-everywhere theorem an intuition rather than treating it as magic. In one dimension, the right derivative is monotone, so nondifferentiability corresponds to jumps. In higher dimensions, the proof reduces directional differentiability to coordinate tests and then intersects full-measure sets. The result explains why ridges are visible but thin.

label: Gradient Continuity Caveats
notes: Separate the strong and weak continuity claims. The gradient is continuous on the differentiability set, and if a finite convex function is differentiable on an entire open convex region, then it is continuously differentiable there. But this does not erase nondifferentiable ridges, and it does not handle boundary behavior without adding the normal cone.

label: Numerical Differentiability Probe
notes: Frame the numerical probe as a diagnostic, not as a proof. Finite differences can identify a candidate gradient on the bowl, but at the absolute value corner they hide the spread of valid supports. The max ridge shows the same problem in two dimensions. The convex certificate is still the singleton subdifferential and the linear directional derivative.

label: Rule Ledger
notes: Use the ledger as the instructor's board summary. Every line has a theorem statement, a visual target, and a known failure mode. The most useful pattern is to move from a proposed gradient to the subdifferential, then to the directional derivative. The almost-everywhere and open-set rules tell students where smoothness can be expected.

label: Recap
notes: Close by returning to the same inspection prompt from the opening slide. To decide differentiability for a convex function, first identify the local supporting slopes. If they form one point, that point is the gradient and all directional derivatives agree with it. If they form a segment, interval, cone, or face, the function is nonsmooth at that point.
